p.src: At that moment, Immortal Luo said, “Disciple, the magic arts you learned in former days are much the same as Gao Lian’s. I shall now transmit to you the True Art of the Celestial Heart and Five Thunderbolts. By practicing it, you can save Song Jiang, safeguard the realm and bring peace to the people, and carry out the Way on Heaven’s behalf. Do not let worldly desires bind you and ruin the great undertaking; devote yourself wholly to the resolve with which you first studied the Way. As for your aged mother, I shall have people attend to her morning and evening, so do not worry about her. You correspond to the Heavenly Leisure Star in the upper realm, and for that reason I permit you to go and aid Song Gongming. I have eight words for you. Remember them well, and do not fail to heed them when the time comes.” Immortal Luo then spoke the eight words: “At Youzhou, halt; upon reaching Bianjing, return.” Gongsun Sheng bowed and received the secret formulas. Then he, Dai Zong, and Li Kui took leave of Immortal Luo, bade farewell to the other Daoist companions, and descended the mountain. Returning home, he made ready his Daoist robes, two precious swords, an iron cap, a ruyi scepter, and the rest. He then bowed farewell to his aged mother, left the mountain, and set out. After they had gone thirty or forty li, Dai Zong said, “I shall go ahead and report to our brother. You, Master, and Li Kui can follow along the main road, and I will come back to meet you.” Gongsun Sheng said, “That will do nicely. Go on ahead and deliver the news, worthy brother; I too shall hasten onward.” Dai Zong instructed Li Kui, “Take good care of the Master on the road. If anything at all goes amiss, you will suffer for it.” Li Kui said, “His magic is every bit as powerful as Immortal Luo’s. How would I dare slight him?” Dai Zong fastened the magic travel talismans to his legs, invoked the Divine Traveling Art, and went on ahead.

p.src: Now Gongsun Sheng and Li Kui left Mount Erxian in Jiugong County and followed the main road, seeking an inn each evening to rest. Li Kui feared Immortal Luo’s magic and waited on Gongsun Sheng with the utmost care, not daring to give rein to his temper. After traveling for three days, the two came to a place called Wugang Town. Seeing the bustling streets crowded with people, Gongsun Sheng said, “These past two days on the road have left us weary. Let us buy a bowl of meatless wine and some vegetarian noodles before we go on.” Li Kui said, “Good.” They saw a small wineshop beside the post road and went inside to sit down. Gongsun Sheng took the place of honor, while Li Kui undid his waist pack and sat below him. They called the waiter to warm some wine and prepare vegetarian dishes for them to eat. Gongsun Sheng asked, “What vegetarian refreshments do you sell here?” The waiter replied, “Our shop sells only wine and meat. We have no vegetarian refreshments, but a household by the marketplace sells date cakes.” Li Kui said, “I will go and buy some.” He took some copper coins from the pack and went straight into the town, where he bought a parcel of date cakes. Just as he was about to return, he heard someone nearby cry out in admiration, “What strength!” When Li Kui looked, he saw a crowd gathered around a burly fellow who was wielding an iron melon-headed hammer, and the onlookers were cheering him.

p.src: Li Kui looked the fellow over. He stood more than seven feet tall, his face was pockmarked, and a broad ridge ran down his nose. When Li Kui examined the iron hammer, he judged that it weighed some thirty catties. Once the man had worked himself into full swing, he brought the melon-headed hammer squarely down on a paving stone and smashed it to powder, drawing cheers from the crowd. Unable to contain himself, Li Kui tucked the date cakes into his bosom and stepped forward to take the iron hammer. The man shouted, “What damned fellow are you? How dare you lay hands on my hammer!” Li Kui said, “What is so damned fine about the way you wield it, that everyone should cheer? The sight of it only fouls a man’s eyes! Watch this master wield it once, and let everyone have a proper look.” The man said, “I will lend it to you. But if you cannot move it, you will take a sound beating about the neck from me before you leave.” Li Kui took the melon-headed hammer and handled it as though he were playing with a pellet. After wielding it for a while, he gently set it down. His face was not flushed, his heart was not pounding, and he was not even short of breath. Seeing this, the man prostrated himself and said, “May I ask my elder brother’s honored name?” Li Kui asked, “Where do you live?” The man replied, “Just up ahead.” He led Li Kui to a place where they found the door secured with a lock. The man unlocked the door with a key and invited Li Kui inside to sit down.

p.src: Li Kui then said, “Fellow, tell me your name so that I may know it.” The man replied, “My humble surname is Tang, and my given name is Long. My father was formerly a stockade commandant in Yan’an Prefecture. Because of his skill at smithing, he won the favor of the Senior Commissioner and was appointed to serve under him. In recent years my father died at his post. I was addicted to gambling and drifted about the rivers and lakes, so for the present I make my living here as a blacksmith. I am passionately fond of wielding spear and staff. Because my whole body is covered in pockmarks, people call me the ‘Gold-Coin Leopard.’ May I ask my elder brother’s honored name?” Li Kui said, “I am Li Kui, the ‘Black Whirlwind,’ one of the heroes of Liangshan Marsh.” Hearing this, Tang Long bowed twice. “I have long heard of your mighty name, brother. Who would have thought I should chance to meet you today?” Li Kui said, “How long will it take you to prosper in a place like this? You would do better to follow me to Liangshan Marsh and join our band. We will make you a chieftain too.” Tang Long said, “If you will not disdain me, brother, and are willing to help me along, I shall gladly follow wherever your whip and stirrup lead.” He then bowed to Li Kui and acknowledged him as his elder brother. Li Kui accepted Tang Long as his younger brother. Tang Long said, “I have neither family nor attendants. Let us go into town and drink three cups of humble wine to mark our sworn brotherhood. We can rest here tonight and set out early tomorrow.” Li Kui said, “My master is waiting at the wineshop up ahead for me to bring back date cakes to eat before we leave. We cannot delay; we must go at once.” Tang Long asked, “Why is it so urgent?” Li Kui said, “You do not know that our elder brother Song Gongming is now fighting on the borders of Gaotangzhou and is waiting only for this master of mine to come to his aid.” Tang Long asked, “Who is this master?” Li Kui said, “Never mind asking. Pack your things quickly and come.” Tang Long hurriedly tied up his bundle, travel money, and silver, put on a felt hat, girded on a saber, and picked up a broad-bladed polearm. Abandoning his dilapidated house and cumbersome old tools, he followed Li Kui straight to the wineshop to meet Gongsun Sheng.

p.src: Gongsun Sheng reproached him, saying, “How could you have been gone so long? Had you come any later, I would have gone away again as before.” Li Kui dared not utter a word in reply. He brought Tang Long forward to bow before Gongsun Sheng and gave a full account of how they had sworn brotherhood. When Gongsun Sheng heard that Tang Long had been a blacksmith, he too was pleased. Li Kui took out the date cakes and told a waiter to prepare them. The three drank several cups of wine together, ate the date cakes, and settled the wine bill. Li Kui and Tang Long each shouldered a bundle, and together with Gongsun Sheng they left Wugang Town and made their winding way toward Gao Tangzhou. On the road they had covered more than two-thirds of the distance when, early that day, they happened to meet Dai Zong coming to receive them. Gongsun Sheng was overjoyed to see him and hurriedly asked, “How has the fighting gone lately?” Dai Zong said, “That scoundrel Gao Lian has lately recovered from his arrow wound and leads his troops out every day to challenge us. Our elder brother is holding fast and dares not engage him, but waits only for your arrival.” Gongsun Sheng said, “That will be easily dealt with.” Li Kui presented Tang Long to Dai Zong, and after explaining all the details, the four men headed together for Gao Tangzhou. Five li from the camp, Lü Fang and Guo Sheng were already waiting to receive them with more than a hundred mounted soldiers. All four mounted horses and rode together to the camp, where Song Jiang, Wu Yong, and the others came out to welcome them. After exchanging courtesies, they laid out a welcoming feast, spoke of all that had passed during their separation, and invited them into the central command tent, where the other chieftains also came to celebrate. Li Kui brought Tang Long forward to pay his respects to Song Jiang, Wu Yong, and all the chieftains. Once the formal courtesies were over, a celebratory banquet was held in the camp.

p.src: The next day in the central command tent, Song Jiang, Wu Yong, and Gongsun Sheng discussed how to defeat Gao Lian. Gongsun Sheng said, “Let the commander issue orders to strike all the camps and move out. We shall see how the enemy responds; this poor Daoist has a plan of his own.” That day Song Jiang sent orders to every camp. All the troops set out together, marched straight to the moat of Gao Tangzhou, and established their camp. At the fifth watch the next morning, food was prepared, and every soldier donned his armor and equipment. Song Gongming, Scholar Wu, and Gongsun Sheng rode three horses straight to the front. Flags waved, drums thundered, men shouted, and gongs rang as the army charged to the foot of the city walls.

p.src: Now Prefect Gao Lian's arrow wound had healed. The night before, a soldier had reported that Song Jiang's forces had returned. In the morning Gao Lian and his men donned their armor, opened the city gate, lowered the drawbridge, and prepared to lead three hundred spirit soldiers and officers of every rank out of the city to meet the enemy. As the two armies drew near, their banners and drums came into sight, and each side deployed its battle formation. In both formations, decorated alligator-hide drums boomed and embroidered banners of many colors fluttered. The gate of Song Jiang's formation opened, and ten horsemen emerged, spreading out on either side like wild-goose wings. The five generals on the left were Hua Rong, Qin Ming, Zhu Tong, Ou Peng, and Lü Fang. The five generals on the right were Lin Chong, Sun Li, Deng Fei, Ma Lin, and Guo Sheng. Of the three horsemen in the center, the foremost was the commander-in-chief, Song Gongming. And how was he arrayed?

p.src: When Prefect Gao Lian reached the front, he shouted fiercely and cursed them: “You bandits from the marsh! Since you have come determined to fight, we shall settle victory and defeat once and for all. Whoever runs away is no true hero!” When Song Jiang heard this, he called out, “Who will ride forth and strike down this villain at once?” Hua Rong, the “Lesser Li Guang,” leveled his spear, spurred his horse, and rode straight to the center of the battlefield. Seeing him, Gao Lian shouted, “Who will go and seize this villain for me?” From among the commandant's troops emerged a champion named Xue Yuanhui. Wielding a pair of sabers and mounted on an inferior horse, he dashed into the center to fight Hua Rong. The two fought several bouts before the formations. Then Hua Rong wheeled his horse and fled toward his own lines. Unaware that it was a ruse, Xue Yuanhui spurred after him at full strength, flourishing both blades. Hua Rong slightly checked his horse, took up his bow, drew an arrow, twisted around in the saddle, and with a single shot sent Xue Yuanhui tumbling headlong from his mount. Both armies raised a thunderous shout. Gao Lian saw this from horseback and flew into a rage. He quickly reached before the saddle bow, took down his bronze plaque embossed with clustered beasts, and struck it with his sword. As soon as he struck it three times, a cloud of yellow sand rose from among the spirit soldiers, shrouding heaven and earth in darkness and blotting out the sun. Amid the rising cries, jackals, wolves, tigers, leopards, monstrous beasts, and venomous creatures came swirling out of the yellow sand. Just as all the soldiers were about to flee, Gongsun Sheng, still on horseback, had already drawn his ancient pine-patterned sword. Pointing it toward the enemy, he muttered an incantation and cried, “Haste!” A shaft of golden light shot forth, and all those monstrous beasts and venomous creatures came tumbling in confusion from the yellow sand before the formation. When the soldiers looked, they saw that they were all tigers, leopards, and other beasts cut from white paper; the yellow sand had completely dispersed and could rise no more. Seeing this, Song Jiang pointed with the tip of his whip, and the entire army, officers and men alike, surged forward to attack. Men fell dead and horses toppled, while banners lay strewn and tangled. Gao Lian hurriedly withdrew his spirit soldiers into the city. Song Jiang's forces pursued them to the walls, but those above hastily hauled up the drawbridge and shut the city gate, then hurled beams and stones down like rain. Song Jiang ordered the gong sounded for withdrawal, gathered his forces, and established camp. After the men had been counted, it was clear that they had won a great victory. Back in his tent, he thanked Master Gongsun for his divine power and virtue, then at once rewarded the whole army for its service.

Unaware that it was a ruse, Xue Yuanhui spurred after him at full strength, flourishing both blades. Hua Rong slightly checked his horse, took up his bow, drew an arrow, twisted around in the saddle, and with a single shot sent Xue Yuanhui tumbling headlong from his mount.
Both armies raised a thunderous shout.
Gao Lian saw this from horseback and flew into a rage. He quickly reached before the saddle bow, took down his bronze plaque embossed with clustered beasts, and struck it with his sword.
As soon as he struck it three times, a cloud of yellow sand rose from among the spirit soldiers, shrouding heaven and earth in darkness and blotting out the sun.
Amid the rising cries, jackals, wolves, tigers, leopards, monstrous beasts, and venomous creatures came swirling out of the yellow sand.

Just as all the soldiers were about to flee, Gongsun Sheng, still on horseback, had already drawn his ancient pine-patterned sword. Pointing it toward the enemy, he muttered an incantation and cried, “Haste!”
A shaft of golden light shot forth, and all those monstrous beasts and venomous creatures came tumbling in confusion from the yellow sand before the formation.
When the soldiers looked, they saw that they were all tigers, leopards, and other beasts cut from white paper; the yellow sand had completely dispersed and could rise no more.
Seeing this, Song Jiang pointed with the tip of his whip, and the entire army, officers and men alike, surged forward to attack.
Men fell dead and horses toppled, while banners lay strewn and tangled.
Gao Lian hurriedly withdrew his spirit soldiers into the city.
Song Jiang's forces pursued them to the walls, but those above hastily hauled up the drawbridge and shut the city gate, then hurled beams and stones down like rain.

Song Jiang ordered the gong sounded for withdrawal, gathered his forces, and established camp. After the men had been counted, it was clear that they had won a great victory. Back in his tent, he thanked Master Gongsun for his divine power and virtue, then at once rewarded the whole army for its service.

p.src: The next day, they divided their forces to surround the city on all four sides and attacked with all their might. Gongsun Sheng said to Song Jiang and Wu Yong, “Although we routed more than half the enemy force last night, we plainly saw those three hundred spirit soldiers retreat into the city. If we press the attack hard today, those villains will surely come to raid our camp tonight. Tonight we should gather the army in one place, then, when the night is deep, send the troops out to lie in ambush on all four sides. Leave only empty tents pitched here, and order the commanders to wait for the thunderclap and the sight of flames rising in the camp, then advance all together.” The orders were duly issued. That day they attacked the city until the hour of the Goat, then withdrew the troops from all four sides to camp, where they loudly beat drums, sounded music, and drank wine. As dusk gradually fell, the chieftains secretly dispersed to their assigned positions and completed their ambushes on all four sides.

p.src: Meanwhile, Song Jiang, Wu Yong, Gongsun Sheng, Hua Rong, Qin Ming, Lü Fang, and Guo Sheng went up an earthen slope to wait. That night, Gao Lian indeed mustered his three hundred spirit soldiers. Each carried an iron gourd on his back, filled with sulfur, saltpeter, and other materials for smoke and fire. Every man wielded a hooked blade or iron broom and held a reed whistle in his mouth. Around the second watch, they threw open the city gate and lowered the drawbridge. Gao Lian led the spirit soldiers forward, with more than thirty horsemen following behind, and charged toward the camp. As they drew near the camp, Gao Lian worked his sorcery from horseback. At once black vapors surged into the sky, a furious wind arose, sand and stones flew, and earth and dust whirled everywhere. The three hundred spirit soldiers each took out a flame and lit the mouth of his gourd. At one blast of their reed whistles, they rolled into the camp through the black vapors, their bodies wreathed in firelight and their great blades and broad axes swinging. On the high ground, Gongsun Sheng wielded his sword and cast a spell, whereupon a thunderclap cracked across the level ground inside the empty camp. The three hundred spirit soldiers hastened to retreat, but flames rose throughout the empty camp, tongues of fire flying wildly until all above and below glowed red, leaving them no way out. The ambushing troops rushed in from all four sides, surrounded the camp palisade, and appeared everywhere out of the darkness. Not one of the three hundred spirit soldiers escaped; all were slain inside the camp. Gao Lian hurriedly led his remaining thirty-odd horsemen back toward the city. A force pursued them from behind, led by Lin Chong, the “Panther Head.” Just as the pursuers were about to overtake them, Gao Lian urgently called for the drawbridge to be lowered. He entered the city with only eight or nine riders; all the others, men and horses alike, were captured alive by Lin Chong. Once inside the city, Gao Lian conscripted all the townspeople to defend the walls. Gao Lian’s regular troops and spirit soldiers had been utterly destroyed by Song Jiang and Lin Chong. The next day, Song Jiang again led his forces to press the siege fiercely from all four sides. Gao Lian thought, “I spent years learning these arts, never imagining they would be broken today. What am I to do now? I have no choice but to send men to seek aid from the neighboring prefectures.” He hurriedly wrote two letters and ordered them taken to Dongchang and Kouzhou. “Neither place is far from here. Both prefects owe their advancement to my elder brother. Tell them to raise troops and come to our aid without delay, traveling day and night.” He assigned two commanding officers from his headquarters to carry the letters, opened the west gate, and had them fight their way out and flee westward. The commanders were about to give chase when Wu Yong issued an order: “Let them go for now. We can turn their own scheme to our advantage.” Song Jiang asked, “What plan do you have in mind, Strategist?” Scholar Wu replied, “The city has few soldiers and officers, which is why he has gone to seek aid. We can send out two forces disguised as relief troops and stage a confused battle along the road. Gao Lian will certainly open the gate and come out to assist them. We can seize the city at once from one side, lure Gao Lian onto a narrow road, and capture him without fail.” Song Jiang was delighted when he heard this. He ordered Dai Zong to return to the Liangshan marsh, fetch two more forces, and bring them by separate routes.

p.src: Meanwhile, every night Gao Lian piled firewood and grass in an open area inside the city and kept a signal fire blazing all night, while the defenders on the walls watched only for the arrival of reinforcements. Several days later, the soldiers defending the city saw Song Jiang’s formations fall into disorder without battle and hurried to report it. On hearing the news, Gao Lian hastily donned his armor and climbed the wall to look. He saw two forces charging toward them amid battle dust that blotted out the sun and cries of slaughter that shook the heavens. The troops besieging the city on all four sides scattered and fled. Convinced that the two relief armies had arrived, Gao Lian mustered every soldier in the city, threw open the gates, and sent them out in separate groups to fall upon the enemy.

p.src: Gao Lian charged up to Song Jiang’s formation and saw Song Jiang riding away along a narrow road with Hua Rong and Qin Ming, the three of them on horseback. Gao Lian led his troops in urgent pursuit, but suddenly heard a rapid volley of cannon fire behind the hillside. Growing suspicious, he turned his troops back. Gongs sounded on both sides. Lü Fang on the left and Guo Sheng on the right each led five hundred troops charging out. When Gao Lian desperately fought his way out, more than half his troops were lost. After escaping the center of the encirclement, he looked toward the city and saw that the walls were already covered with the banners of Liangshan Marsh. Looking around once more, he saw that there were no relief troops anywhere. With no other choice, he led his few routed survivors down a secluded mountain path. Before they had gone ten li, a formidable band of troops burst out from behind the mountain. At their head rode Sun Li, the “Sick Yuchi,” who blocked the way and shouted fiercely, “I have waited long for you! Dismount quietly and submit to binding!” Gao Lian turned his troops back, but another formidable force had already blocked the road behind him. At its head, mounted on horseback, was Zhu Tong, the “Lord of the Beautiful Beard.” Attacked from both ends and cut off on every side, Gao Lian abandoned his mount and fled up the mountain. The troops all around pursued him up the mountain. In his panic, Gao Lian muttered an incantation and cried, “Rise!” Riding upon a mass of black cloud, he slowly rose into the air and flew straight to the mountaintop. Just then Gongsun Sheng emerged from beside the slope. On seeing this, he raised his sword from horseback and worked his art toward the sky, likewise muttering an incantation before crying, “Swift!” He pointed his sword upward, and Gao Lian came tumbling headlong out of the cloud. Lei Heng, the “Winged Tiger,” darted in from the side and cut Gao Lian in two with a single sweep of his broad-bladed saber. Alas, a lord honored with chariots and horses became but a man within a fleeting dream. A poem bears witness:

p.src: Above, Heaven’s mirror looks down upon all; below, the spirits of earth observe all. In the light, the sovereign’s law follows close; in the dark, ghosts and spirits attend. Those who commit violence meet violence in the end; those who trust in power return at last to powerlessness. I urge you to guard yourself throughout your life: how lamentable, how alarming, how fearsome!

p.src: Lei Heng carried the severed head down the mountain with the others and first sent a man ahead at full speed to report to the commander. Song Jiang, already informed that Gao Lian had been killed, gathered his troops and entered the city of Gaotangzhou. His first military order was: “Do not harm the common people.” At the same time, he posted proclamations to reassure the populace and forbade his troops from taking so much as a hair. Then he went to the main prison to rescue Lord Chai. By then, the wardens in charge of the prison and the jail guards had all fled. Only thirty or fifty prisoners remained; their cangues and shackles were all removed, and every one of them was released. Yet Lord Chai alone was nowhere among them. Song Jiang was deeply troubled. Searching further, they came to a cell where Chai Huangcheng’s entire household, old and young, was imprisoned; in another prison were the members of Chai Jin’s household who had been arrested and brought from Cangzhou, all confined together there. Because fighting had continued for days, they had not yet been interrogated or sentenced—but still no one could discover where Lord Chai was.

p.src: When Wu the Scholar ordered the gaolers and warders of Gaotangzhou Prison to be assembled and questioned, one of them stepped forward and reported: “I am Lin Ren, a prison warden. The other day Prefect Gao Lian assigned me especially to keep Chai Jin under close guard and allow no mishap. He further instructed me, ‘Whether the news be good or bad, you may finish him off at once.’ Three days ago, Prefect Gao Lian wanted Chai Jin brought out to be put to death. Seeing that he was a fine and worthy man, I could not bear to do it, so I merely claimed, ‘The prisoner is gravely ill—eight parts gone already—so there is no need to act.’ Later, when they pressed me more urgently, I replied that Chai Jin was already dead. Because fighting had continued for days, the prefect had no leisure to attend to it; but I feared he might send someone down to inspect the prisoner, in which case I would certainly be punished. Yesterday I led Chai Jin to the dry well behind the prison, removed his cangue and fetters, and lowered him inside to hide. I do not know whether he is alive or dead now.”

p.src: On hearing this, Song Jiang hastily ordered Lin Ren to lead them inside. They went straight to the dry well behind the prison and peered down. Its interior was pitch-black, and no one could tell how deep it was. They called from above, but no answer came. When they lowered a rope to gauge it, they found the well to be some eighty or ninety feet deep. Song Jiang said, “It seems certain that Lord Chai is most likely dead.” Tears ran down Song Jiang’s cheeks. Wu the Scholar said, “Commander, do not grieve just yet. If someone dares go down and investigate, we shall know whether he is there or not.” Before he had finished speaking, Li Kui, the Black Whirlwind, came around and shouted, “Let me go down!” Song Jiang said, “Excellent. It was you who brought this calamity upon him in the first place; today is the proper time to make amends.” Li Kui laughed and said, “I am not afraid to go down, but mind you do not cut the rope!” Wu the Scholar said, “You truly are a sly one.” They fetched a large bamboo basket, bound ropes around it, joined them to make a long line, erected a frame, and hung the rope over it. Li Kui stripped stark naked, took an axe in each hand, and sat in the basket. They lowered him into the well, with two bronze bells fastened to the rope. When they had gradually lowered him to the bottom, Li Kui climbed out of the basket and felt around. His hands came upon a heap, but it was a pile of bones. Li Kui exclaimed, “Mother and father! What the devil is this doing here?” He felt his way over to the other side, but the bottom there was soaking wet and offered nowhere to set his feet. Li Kui thrust both axes into the basket and explored below with both hands. The well widened out on every side, and as he groped about he touched a man crouched in a heap in a pool of water. Li Kui called, “Lord Chai!” There was no movement. When Li Kui felt him with his hand, he heard only the faintest moan coming from his mouth. Li Kui said, “Thank Heaven and Earth! If that is so, he can still be saved!” He immediately climbed into the basket and shook the bronze bells, whereupon the men above hauled him up. After Li Kui told them what he had found below, Song Jiang said, “Go down once more. Put Lord Chai into the basket and send him up first; then we shall lower the basket again to fetch you.” Li Kui said, “Elder Brother, you do not know that I was tricked twice on my trip to Jizhou. I will not fall for it a third time!” Song Jiang laughed. “How could I ever play such a trick on you? Hurry down.” Li Kui had no choice but to sit in the basket again and descend into the well.

p.src: When he reached the bottom, Li Kui climbed out of the basket, took Lord Chai in his arms, placed him inside, and shook the bronze bells on the rope. The men above heard the signal and promptly hauled the basket up. When it reached the top, everyone was overjoyed at the sight. Song Jiang saw that Chai Jin’s head and forehead were split open, the flesh of both legs had been beaten to a pulp, and his eyes opened a little only to close again. Song Jiang was deeply distressed and ordered a physician summoned to treat him. Meanwhile, Li Kui was shouting and bellowing at the bottom of the well. Hearing him, Song Jiang hastily ordered the basket lowered to bring him up. When Li Kui reached the top, he burst out angrily: “You are no good men either! You nearly failed to lower the basket and save me!” Song Jiang said, “We were wholly occupied with caring for Lord Chai and forgot about you. Do not blame us.” Song Jiang then ordered the men to carry Chai Jin to a cart and lay him down. The dependents of both households and the great quantity of recovered family property filled more than twenty carts; he ordered Li Kui and Lei Heng to escort them ahead to Liangshan Marsh. Gao Lian’s entire household, high and low, some thirty or forty souls, were beheaded in the marketplace. Lin Ren was rewarded and thanked. All the money and valuables in the government treasury, the grain and rice in the granaries, and Gao Lian’s household possessions were loaded up and taken to the mountain. The officers and commanders, great and small, departed Gaotangzhou and returned victorious to Liangshan Marsh. They did not harm so much as an autumn hair in any prefecture or county through which they passed. After several days on the road, they returned to the great stronghold. Chai Jin rose from his sickbed and expressed his thanks to Lords Chao and Song and all the chieftains. Chao Gai ordered a separate house built for Lord Chai near Song Gongming’s quarters on the mountaintop, so that Chai Jin and his family might live there. Chao Gai, Song Jiang, and all the others rejoiced greatly. With the return from Gaotangzhou, Chai Jin and Tang Long were added to their company as two new chieftains. A celebratory banquet was held, but of that there is no need to speak further.

p.src: Now to speak of Dongchang and Kouzhou: when both places learned that Gao Lian had been killed and Gaotangzhou had fallen, they had no choice but to compose memorials and send messengers to report the matter to the imperial court. Officials who had fled the disaster at Gaotangzhou also reached the capital and gave a full account of what had happened. When Grand Marshal Gao heard the news, he learned that his brother Gao Lian had been killed. At the fifth watch the next morning, he waited in the Courtyard of the Awaiting Dawn specifically for the Jingyang Bell to sound. The hundred officials, each arrayed in court dress, proceeded to the vermilion steps and waited for the imperial audience. At the third division of the fifth watch that day, the Daoist Sovereign Emperor ascended the throne hall. The ceremonial whip cracked three times, and the civil and military ranks stood in perfect order. When the Son of Heaven had taken his seat, the master of ceremonies called out, “Those with business, leave your ranks and present your memorials; if there is no business, roll up the screen and close the audience.” Grand Marshal Gao stepped from his rank and memorialized: “The rebel chiefs Chao Gai and Song Jiang of Liangshan Marsh in Jizhou have repeatedly committed great crimes, assaulting cities, plundering granaries, and gathering murderous villains into their band. They have killed government troops in Jizhou, thrown Jiangzhou and Wuwei Commandery into turmoil, and now have slaughtered the officials and people of Gaotangzhou to the last and carried off everything in its granaries and treasuries. This is a mortal danger at the very heart of the realm. Unless they are exterminated without delay, their rebel power will grow until it becomes impossible to subdue. I humbly beg Your Majesty to decide.” The emperor was greatly alarmed by the memorial and immediately issued an edict appointing Grand Marshal Gao to select commanders and mobilize troops to suppress the rebels. He was to clear the marsh completely and exterminate their kind. Grand Marshal Gao submitted further: “For mere bandits such as these, there is no need to raise a great army. I recommend one man who can go and recover the territory.” The emperor said, “If he is recommended by you, there can surely be no mistake. Order him to set out at once. Should swift dispatches announce his success, he shall be raised in office, bestowed rewards, and appointed to high position.” Grand Marshal Gao memorialized: “This man is a direct descendant of Huyan Zan, the renowned general of Hedong from the founding years of our dynasty. His personal name is Zhuo. He wields two bronze clubs and possesses courage that ten thousand men could not withstand. He presently serves as supreme military commander of Runing Commandery and has many elite soldiers and valiant officers under his command. I recommend this man as capable of campaigning against and suppressing Liangshan Marsh. He may be appointed Military Commissioner, given command of elite horse and foot soldiers, and ordered to clear the mountain stronghold by a fixed date and return victorious to court.” The emperor approved the memorial and issued an edict: “Have the Bureau of Military Affairs immediately send a man bearing this decree to Runingzhou, and summon him here with all speed, traveling day and night.” After the audience ended that day, Grand Marshal Gao returned to his headquarters and had the Bureau of Military Affairs assign an officer to carry the imperial edict and deliver the summons. The officer departed that very day, with a strict deadline by which Huyan Zhuo was to reach the capital and receive his orders.

p.src: Now Huyan Zhuo was holding court at the Military Command Office in Ruzhou when an attendant reported, “An imperial envoy has come expressly to summon you to the capital. There is an important commission for you.” Huyan Zhuo and the prefecture’s officials went beyond the city walls to receive the envoy and escorted him to the Military Command Office. After the edict had been read, they held a banquet for the envoy. Huyan Zhuo then hurriedly made ready his helmet and armor, saddle and horse, weapons and equipment, and, taking thirty or forty attendants with him, departed Ruzhou in the envoy’s company and hastened toward the capital by night and day. Nothing of note occurred along the way. Before long he reached the capital, dismounted before the Palace Commandant’s Office, and went in to see Grand Marshal Gao. That day Gao Qiu was holding court in the Palace Commandant’s Office when a gate official reported, “Huyan Zhuo, summoned from Ruzhou, is now waiting outside.” Grand Marshal Gao was delighted and ordered Huyan Zhuo to be admitted to pay his respects. p.src: Descended from a founding hero, Great-grandson of a valiant general of the former reign; His family’s art of the whips is wondrous beyond compare, Heroic and martial, he is seasoned in battle. p.src: When Grand Marshal Gao had finished asking after him, he bestowed rewards upon him. At the morning audience the next day, he presented Huyan Zhuo to the Daoist Emperor. Emperor Huizong saw that Huyan Zhuo was a man of uncommon bearing and was greatly pleased. He forthwith presented him with a horse called Snow-Kicking Black Steed. The horse’s whole body was black as an ink-stick, while its four hooves were white as snowy silk; hence its name, Snow-Kicking Black Steed. It could cover a thousand li in a day, and by imperial decree it was given to Huyan Zhuo as his mount. After Huyan Zhuo had expressed his gratitude for the imperial favor, he accompanied Grand Marshal Gao back to the Palace Commandant’s Office to discuss raising an army to suppress the outlaws of Liangshan Marsh. Huyan Zhuo said, “I beg leave to report to Your Excellency: from what I have learned, Liangshan Marsh has many troops and numerous commanders, all highly skilled in arms. We must neither take the enemy lightly nor underestimate them. I ask permission to recommend two commanders to serve as the vanguard. If they lead the troops there with me, we shall surely win great merit.” Grand Marshal Gao was delighted to hear this and asked, “Whom do you recommend to command the vanguard?” Huyan Zhuo’s recommendation of these two commanders was destined to bring more fine warriors into Wanzi City and lead Liangshan Marsh to inflict a crushing defeat upon the imperial army. Before their deeds had earned them a place in the Pavilion of Soaring Mist, their names would first be inscribed in the Hall of Righteous Assembly. But just whom did Huyan Zhuo recommend to Grand Marshal Gao? Listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
